input:
it is a remarkable and extremely useful feature of the transfer processes that the same boundary-layer structure which governs the friction experienced by a surface also governs the rate at which a species is transferred across that layer, and this correspondence is captured by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, which states the relationship in the elegantly simple form $j_D$ = $f/2$. It should be emphasised that the quantity on the right-hand side of this expression is not obtained by fitting mass-transfer data at all; rather, it is taken directly from the friction behaviour of the same surface, so that friction is treated as the known quantity and the transfer coefficient as the quantity to be predicted.

A short numerical check helps to illustrate the magnitude of the prediction involved. At $Re$ = 20000, the friction relation developed in the earlier section gives $f$ = 0.0064 for the smooth surface under consideration, and the analogy then yields $j_D$ = 0.0032 for the transfer of a species to that surface under the same flow conditions. This check is, in essence, a consistency check on the two definitions rather than a measurement in its own right, demonstrating what the analogy commits the transfer coefficient to once the friction behaviour has been fixed.

Having said that, the analogy does break down in situations where the drag on the surface is not attributable to skin friction alone. On rough surfaces, and around bluff shapes placed in the flow, a significant part of the measured drag is pressure drag acting on the roughness elements or on the separated wake, and this component has no real counterpart in the transfer of a species to the surface. In such cases the measured $f$ includes a contribution that $j_D$ cannot follow, and the equality consequently tends to overstate the transfer coefficient, which is an important limitation to bear in mind when applying the analogy in practice.

the same boundary-layer structure that sets the friction on a surface also sets the rate at which a species crosses that layer, and the Chilton-Colburn analogy states the correspondence in its simplest form: $j_D$ = $f/2$. The quantity on the right is not fitted to mass-transfer data. It is taken over from the friction behaviour of the same surface, and the analogy is used in that direction throughout this chapter: friction is the measured or correlated quantity, and the transfer coefficient is the predicted one.

A short check shows the size of the prediction. At $Re$ = 20000, the friction relation of the earlier section gives $f$ = 0.0064 for the smooth surface, and the analogy then gives $j_D$ = 0.0032 for the transfer of a species to that surface under the same flow. The check is a consistency check on the two definitions rather than a measurement. It shows what the analogy commits the transfer coefficient to once the friction behaviour has been fixed, and a measured coefficient that departs from the predicted value is evidence about the analogy, not about the arithmetic.

The analogy fails where the drag on the surface is not skin friction alone. On a rough surface, and around bluff shapes set in the flow, part of the measured drag is pressure drag on the roughness elements or on the separated wake behind the shape, and that part has no counterpart in the transfer of a species to the surface. The measured value of $f$ then carries a contribution that $j_D$ cannot follow, and the equality overstates the transfer coefficient. The correspondence also presumes that the velocity layer and the concentration layer develop in the same way along the surface; where the two layers grow under different conditions, the simple equality is not available even on a smooth surface, and the analogy is replaced by a correlation fitted to transfer data.
